source_text: οἵδε μὲν οἱ χρόνοι τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι πρεσβυτάτων σοφῶν τε καὶ φιλοσόφων. ὡς δὲ οἱ πλεῖστοι αὐτῶν βάρβαροι τὸ γένος καὶ παρὰ βαρβάροις παιδευθέντες, τί δεῖ καὶ λέγειν, εἰ γε Τυρρηνὸς ἢ Τύριος ὁ Πυθαγόρας ἐδείκνυτο, Ἀντισθένης δὲ Φρὺξ ἦν καὶ Ὀρφεὺς Οδρύσης ἢ Θρᾷξ; Ὅμηρον γὰρ οἱ πλεῖστοι Αἰγύπτιον φαίνουσιν. Θαλῆς δὲ Φοῖνιξ ὢν τὸ γένος καὶ τοῖς Αἰγυπτίων προφήταις συμβεβληκέναι εἴρηται, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Πυθαγόρας αὐτοῖς γε τούτοις, δἰ οὓς καὶ περιετέμετο, ἵνα δὴ καὶ εἰς τὰ ἄδυτα κατελθὼν τὴν μυστικὴν παρ’ Αἰγυπτίων ἐκμάθοι φιλοσοφίαν, Χαλδαίων τε καὶ Μάγων τοῖς ἀρίστοις συνεγένετο καὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν νῦν οὕτω καλουμένην τὸ παρ’ αὐτῷ ὁμακοεῖον αἰνίττεται. Πλάτων δὲ οὐκ ἀρνεῖται τὰ κάλλιστα εἰς φιλοσοφίαν παρὰ τῶν βαρβάρων ἐμπορεύεσθαι εἴς τε Αἴγυπτον ἀφικέσθαι ὁμολογεῖ. δύνασθαι γοῦν ἐν τῷ Φαίδωνί φησι πανταχόθεν τὸν φιλόσοφον ὠφελεῖσθαι γράφων· πολλὴ μὲν ἡ Ἑλλάς, ἔφη, ὦ Κέβης, ἦ δ’ ὅς, ἐν ᾗ εἰσι πάμπαν ἀγαθοὶ ἄνδρες, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τὰ τῶν βαρβάρων γένη. οὕτως οἴεται ὁ Πλάτων καὶ βαρβάρων φιλοσόφους τινὰς εἶναι, ὁ δὲ Ἐπίκουρος ἔμπαλιν ὑπολαμβάνει μόνους φιλοσοφῆσαι Ἕλληνας δύνασθαι. ἔν τε τῷ Συμποσίῳ ἐπαινῶν Πλάτων τοὺς βαρβάρους ὡς διαφερόντως ἀσκήσαντας † μόνους ἀληθῶς φησι καὶ ἄλλοι ἄλλοθι πολλαχοῦ καὶ ἐν Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις, ὧν καὶ ἱερὰ πολλὰ ἤδη γέγονε διὰ τοὺς τοιούτους παῖδας. δῆλοι δέ εἰσιν οἱ βάρβαροι διαφερόντως τιμήσαντες τοὺς αὐτῶν νομοθέτας τε καὶ διδασκάλους θεοὺς προσειπόντες. ψυχὰς γὰρ ἀγαθὰς κατὰ Πλάτωνα καταλιπούσας τὸν ὑπερουράνιον τόπον ὑπομεῖναι ἐλθεῖν εἰς τόνδε τὸν τάρταρον καὶ σῶμα ἀναλαβούσας τῶν ἐν γενέσει κακῶν ἁπάντων μετασχεῖν ὑπολαμβάνουσι, κηδομένας τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους, αἳ νόμους τε ἔθεσαν καὶ φιλοσοφίαν ἐκήρυξαν, οὗ μεῖζον ἀγαθὸν τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένει οὔτ’ ἦλθέν ποτε ἐκ θεῶν οὔτ’ ἀφίξεται. καὶ μοι δοκοῦσιν αἰσθόμενοι τῆς μεγάλης εὐποιίας τῆς διὰ τῶν σοφῶν σεβασθῆναί τε τοὺς ἄνδρας καὶ δημοσίᾳ φιλοσοφῆσαι.
pass_a_gloss: These indeed are the times of the oldest wise men and philosophers among the Greeks. But since most of them are of barbarian race and were educated among barbarians, what need is there to say, if Pythagoras was shown to be a Tyrrhenian or a Tyrian, and Antisthenes was a Phrygian and Orpheus an Odrysian or a Thracian? For most people think Homer was an Egyptian. And Thales, being a Phoenician by race, is said to have associated with the prophets of the Egyptians, just like Pythagoras with these same people, through whom he also was circumcised, so that he might go down into the innermost sanctum and learn the mystical philosophy of the Egyptians. And he became acquainted with the most excellent Chaldeans and Magi, and he hints at the church now so called, which was the gathering place with him. Plato does not deny that the most beautiful things in philosophy were imported from the barbarians, and he admits to having gone to Egypt. For in the Phaedo he says that the philosopher can be benefited from everywhere, writing: 'Greece is a large place, O Cebes, where there are altogether good men, and there are many good things among the barbarian nations.' Thus Plato thinks that there are also philosophers among the barbarians, but Epicurus, on the other hand, thinks that only Greeks can philosophize. And in the Symposium, Plato praises the barbarians as having excelled in their practice, and he says truly, and others elsewhere, both among Greeks and barbarians, whose sacred things have already been established through such children. The barbarians are clearly those who have especially honored their own lawgivers and teachers, calling them gods. For they think that good souls, according to Plato, having left the heavenly place, came into this underworld and, having taken on bodies, shared in all the evils of generation, being concerned for the human race, which established laws and proclaimed philosophy, which is the greatest good that has come or will come to the human race from the gods. And it seems to me that, perceiving the great benefit that has been conferred through the wise men, they have revered these men and philosophized publicly.
pass_b_english: Here we have the dates of the earliest Greek sages and philosophers. Yet since most of them were of barbarian stock and were educated among barbarians, what more need be said? Pythagoras is shown to have been a Tyrrhenian or a Tyrian, Antisthenes a Phrygian, Orpheus an Odrysian or a Thracian. Most people even consider Homer an Egyptian. Thales, a Phoenician by birth, is said to have associated with the prophets of the Egyptians, just as Pythagoras did with those same men. It was through them that Pythagoras was circumcised, so that he could enter the inner sanctum and learn the Egyptians’ mystical philosophy. He also became intimate with the most eminent Chaldeans and Magi, and he hints at the assembly now so called, which was the meeting-place in his own circle.

Plato does not deny that the finest elements of philosophy were imported from the barbarians, and he admits that he himself went to Egypt. In the Phaedo he writes that the philosopher can profit from every quarter: ‘Greece is large, Cebes, and in it there are thoroughly good men; many good things also exist among the barbarian nations.’ Thus Plato believes there are philosophers among the barbarians, whereas Epicurus holds the opposite view, that only Greeks can philosophize. In the Symposium Plato praises the barbarians for having excelled in their practice, and he says truly—as do others elsewhere, both among Greeks and barbarians—whose sacred rites have already been established through such children.

The barbarians are clearly those who especially honored their own lawgivers and teachers by calling them gods. For they believed that good souls, according to Plato, left the heavenly realm, descended into this underworld, took on bodies, and so shared in all the evils of mortal life. They did this out of concern for the human race, establishing laws and proclaiming philosophy—the greatest good that has ever come or ever will come to humanity from the gods. And it seems to me that, perceiving the great benefit conferred through the wise, they revered those men and philosophized publicly.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex clauses regarding Pythagoras's circumcision and the Platonic view of souls. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source. Scripture references (Phaedo and Symposium) are correctly identified as literary works rather than biblical verses, and the internal logic of the argument is preserved.
